questiontext.text: According to this course's Environment Setup module, why does WSL2 support kernel-level features like proper permission bits and systemd, while WSL1 did not?

answer.text: WSL2 runs an actual Linux kernel inside a lightweight virtual machine; WSL1 translated Linux system calls into Windows equivalents instead of running a real kernel
WSL2 requires a newer version of Windows that added native Linux driver support at the hardware level
WSL1 lacked a graphical interface, which systemd and permission bits both depend on
WSL2 installs a full Ubuntu Desktop environment by default, while WSL1 only installs a command-line-only distribution

questiontext.text: Per this course's Linux Fundamentals module, what is the role of the kernel?

answer.text: The core program that manages a computer's hardware and mediates every other program's access to it
The program that reads a trainee's typed commands and asks the kernel to execute them
A specific bundle of the kernel, package manager, and default tools, such as Ubuntu or Fedora
A terminal emulator window that displays typed keystrokes

questiontext.text:
A trainee runs the following command, intending to add a new line to an existing log file:

echo "new entry" > existing_log.txt

What actually happens to existing_log.txt?

answer.text: Its previous contents are overwritten (destroyed) before "new entry" is written
"new entry" is appended after the file's existing content, leaving prior lines intact
The shell refuses to run the command because the file already exists
The shell prompts for confirmation before overwriting the file

questiontext.text: Per the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard as taught in this course, what belongs under /var?

answer.text: Variable data that changes at runtime, such as logs and spool files
System-wide configuration files, almost always in plain text
Personal directories for each non-root user
The bulk of installed user programs and their supporting files

questiontext.text: Per this course's file-viewing module, which command is the standard way to watch a log file update in real time while a service is actively running?

answer.text: Repeatedly running cat on the file
less, left open without following mode
grep alone, run once against the file

questiontext.text: Per this course's Permissions module, why is setting a script's permissions to 777 "just to get it working" explicitly discouraged?

answer.text: It grants write access to every user on the system, a common root cause of later security incidents
It makes the script noticeably slower to execute due to extra permission checks
It prevents the script from being scheduled by cron
It only affects the file's group ownership, not who can read or write it

name.text: LT07 — apt update vs apt install

questiontext.text: Per this course's Package Management module, what does running sudo apt update actually do?

answer.text: Refreshes the local list of available packages and versions, without installing or upgrading anything by itself
Installs the latest available version of every currently installed package
Installs whichever package name is given as the next argument
Removes packages that are no longer needed by any installed software

questiontext.text: A trainee's script runs correctly every time it's triggered manually from the terminal, but appears to "do nothing" when run on its cron schedule. Per this course's Processes, systemd & Cron module, what is the most likely cause?

answer.text: A relative path or missing environment variable that only existed in the trainee's interactive shell, not cron's minimal environment
The crontab entry uses the wrong number of asterisks in its schedule field
The script was never made executable with chmod
systemd is not installed on the machine

name.text: LT09 — Purpose of an Exit Code

questiontext.text: Per this course's Shell Scripting module, why must a script call exit with an explicit status code (e.g. exit 1) at every exit point, including its error paths?

answer.text: A caller such as cron, systemd, or Kubernetes checks the exit code to determine whether the script succeeded or failed
It determines how much memory the script is allowed to use while running
It is only used to print a message to the terminal after the script finishes
It is required by Bash syntax and has no effect on how the script is treated afterward

questiontext.text: Per this course's Security & Secrets Hygiene module, what should happen to a credential that was once hardcoded into a script and committed to Git, even after that line is later removed from the file?

answer.text: It should be treated as compromised and rotated (replaced with a new credential), since Git history still contains it
Nothing further is needed once the line is deleted from the current version of the file
It only needs to be rotated if the repository is public
Renaming the environment variable that holds it is sufficient to prevent exposure
